events.title: Spinning Jenny Invented
events.blurb: A Lancashire weaver, semi-literate and working out of his home, built a hand-cranked multi-spindle spinning frame that let one operator spin eight threads simultaneously rather than one. Later versions spun up to 120 spindles at once. Other weavers' wives in the district, seeing their cottage-industry spinning work disappearing, broke into his house and smashed his prototypes. He patented the invention six years later.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1764 — James Hargreaves in Blackburn, England. Patented 1770. The name "Jenny" is probably derived from "gin," a contemporary term for a mechanical engine — not, contrary to popular story, after his daughter. Hargreaves died in poverty in 1778.

events.title: Great Exhibition Opens
events.blurb: Queen Victoria opened a five-month international exhibition of industrial and artistic products housed in a vast prefabricated iron-and-glass structure in Hyde Park — the building nicknamed the "Crystal Palace." 14,000 exhibitors from 25 countries displayed 100,000 exhibits; six million visitors paid admission. The exhibition's organizer, Prince Albert, had intended it as both a celebration of industrial progress and a showcase for the superiority of free trade. It made a healthy profit, used to found London museums.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1851 — Prince Albert's Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations. Designer Joseph Paxton, a gardener turned architect, had designed the building in a single afternoon on a sheet of blotting paper. The profit funded the Victoria and Albert, Science, and Natural History museums.

events.title: Coca-Cola Invented
events.blurb: An Atlanta pharmacist, a former Confederate officer who had become addicted to morphine following a Civil War injury, mixed a flavoured syrup of coca leaves and kola nuts with carbonated water at a downtown soda fountain and began selling it by the glass as a "brain tonic." The formula initially contained a small amount of cocaine; it was removed in 1903. The modestly popular local beverage grew into the world's most recognized consumer brand.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1886 — John Pemberton at Jacobs' Pharmacy, Atlanta. Pemberton sold the formula piecemeal in ill health; Asa Griggs Candler consolidated ownership and built the business. Coca-Cola's secret recipe, "Merchandise 7X," is supposedly known to only two executives at any time.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: First Moving Assembly Line
events.blurb: A Detroit automobile company introduced a moving chassis-assembly line at its Highland Park plant, cutting the time needed to assemble a car from 12 hours to 93 minutes. The innovation — borrowed in part from Chicago meatpacking "disassembly" lines — let the company slash prices and dramatically increase production. The line's relentless pace was hated by workers; the company had to double wages the following year to keep them on the job.
events.revealBlurb: December 1, 1913 — Ford Motor Company, Highland Park plant. The $5/day wage (equivalent to about $140/day today) followed on January 5, 1914. Workers' turnover at the plant dropped from 370 percent annually to near zero. The wage offer drew applicants by the thousands; police had to turn away crowds in a near-riot.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: iMac Released
events.blurb: A California computer company, newly returned to profitability under a recently returned co-founder, released an all-in-one desktop machine housed in a translucent Bondi-blue plastic case, with no floppy drive, a built-in USB port, and a round puck of a mouse. Industrial designer Jonathan Ive had led the design. The machine was derided on spec by some industry press; it sold over 800,000 units in the first five months and rescued the company's consumer business.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1998 — Apple iMac G3, designed by Jonathan Ive under Steve Jobs. The "i" prefix, coined by copywriter Ken Segall, would carry over to iPod, iPhone, iPad, iCloud. The translucent plastic shell was revolutionary for its time.

events.title: GPS Civilian Access Improved
events.blurb: At midnight, Washington time, the U.S. Department of Defense turned off a feature called Selective Availability, which had deliberately degraded civilian GPS signals by up to 100 metres. The next morning, civilian receivers everywhere in the world suddenly had ten-times-better accuracy — 10 metres instead of 100. The change unlocked a generation of new commercial uses: in-car navigation, smartphone maps, precision agriculture, geocaching, and eventually app-dispatched taxi services.
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 2000 — directed by President Bill Clinton. The signal had been degraded during the Cold War for fear of hostile actors targeting US assets. The 2007 iPhone's eventual GPS feature depended entirely on this unlock.

events.title: iPod Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a white portable music player with a 5 GB hard drive — "1,000 songs in your pocket," according to its co-founder's introduction — and a scrollwheel for navigation. The industry press was unimpressed; smaller MP3 players already existed. Over the next decade, the iPod and its derivatives would sell over 400 million units, reshape the music industry, and serve as a forerunner and technological foundation for the iPhone.
events.revealBlurb: October 23, 2001 — Apple iPod. Steve Jobs introduced it at a small press event, not to a large keynote crowd. Initial reviews focused on how it was Mac-only; the 2003 Windows version opened the floodgates.

events.title: AlphaGo Beats Lee Sedol
events.blurb: A London-based artificial intelligence laboratory's go-playing program, trained on millions of human games and then on games it had played against itself, defeated the reigning world champion of the ancient Asian board game 4–1 in a five-game match in Seoul. The match was broadcast live to 280 million people. Experts had predicted a champion-beating go program was a decade away; the algorithmic gap between games like chess and go had seemed insurmountable.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 2016 — DeepMind's AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol. Lee's single winning game, move 78 — the "divine move" — exploited a subtle blind spot in the AI. DeepMind was acquired by Google in 2014 for around $500 million. Lee retired from professional go three years later, partly because AI had changed the game.

events.title: Hippocratic Oath Composed
events.blurb: Greek medical writers associated with a physician teaching on an Aegean island composed a short ethical oath addressed to Apollo and Asclepius, binding physicians to care for their patients, respect their teachers, preserve patient confidences, and do no harm. The document is arguably the oldest surviving code of professional ethics. Modern versions, substantially modified, are still sworn by many medical-school graduates.
events.revealBlurb: c. 400 BCE — attributed to Hippocrates of Kos, though probably composed by his students or school. The modern "first, do no harm" is actually not in the original Greek text; it appears later in Hippocrates' Epidemics. The oath still shows up at white-coat ceremonies.

events.title: Semmelweis and Handwashing
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Hungarian-born obstetrician in a Vienna maternity hospital observed that the ward staffed by medical students (who also performed autopsies) had a puerperal-fever death rate three times higher than the ward staffed by midwives. He instituted compulsory chlorinated-lime handwashing and watched the death rate drop tenfold. The medical establishment rejected his findings; he was dismissed, ridiculed, and eventually committed to an asylum, where he died of injuries from a beating by guards.
events.revealBlurb: 1847 — Ignaz Semmelweis at Vienna General Hospital. His theory was resisted because germ theory didn't yet exist; doctors took offense at being blamed for patient deaths. He died in an asylum on August 13, 1865, ironically of an infection from his beating injuries. Germ theory vindicated him a few years later.

events.title: Snow's Cholera Pump
events.blurb: A London physician, investigating a cholera outbreak in a Soho neighbourhood that had killed 127 people in three days, mapped the cases and traced their common origin to a public water pump on Broad Street. He persuaded the local parish authorities to remove the pump's handle. New cases stopped almost immediately. His investigation established that cholera was a water-borne disease — against the reigning theory that it spread through "miasmas" in the air.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1854 — John Snow, Soho, London. His sketched map of the cases clustered around the pump is a founding document of epidemiology. The pump's water source had been contaminated by a nearby cesspit. A replica pump stands at the site today, with its handle symbolically removed.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: WHO Certifies Smallpox Eradication
events.blurb: The World Health Assembly certified the global eradication of smallpox — the only human infectious disease ever deliberately driven to extinction — following a 13-year WHO campaign using ring vaccination to contain and eliminate every remaining outbreak. The last naturally occurring case had been recorded in Somalia in 1977, ending a disease that had killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racially segregated public schools are "inherently unequal" and therefore unconstitutional, overturning the 58-year-old "separate but equal" doctrine. The narrow ruling on schools would expand over the next decade to strike down segregation in parks, beaches, swimming pools, and every other public facility.
events.revealBlurb: May 17, 1954 — Chief Justice Earl Warren assembled a 9-0 majority despite internal resistance. Enforcement took years; Arkansas governors called out the national guard to bar Black students, and some counties closed their schools entirely rather than integrate.

events.title: Freedom Riders Depart
events.blurb: Thirteen volunteers — seven Black, six white — boarded buses in Washington, D.C. bound for New Orleans to test a recent Supreme Court ruling outlawing segregated interstate travel facilities. In Alabama their bus was firebombed outside Anniston and the riders beaten bloody by a mob in Birmingham. They kept riding. Subsequent waves continued through the summer.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1961 — sponsored by CORE. A 21-year-old John Lewis was among them and had his skull fractured. Attorney General Robert Kennedy called for a "cooling-off period;" CORE leader James Farmer replied: "We've been cooling off for 100 years."

events.title: Birmingham Children's Crusade
events.blurb: Over several days in a notoriously segregated Alabama steel city, more than a thousand Black schoolchildren — some as young as 6 — marched out of classes in organized protest. Police commissioner Bull Connor ordered fire hoses and attack dogs deployed against them. Photographs of a teenage boy lunged at by a German shepherd appeared on front pages across the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 2-5, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. King agreed to use children over the objections of many advisers; they were less vulnerable to losing jobs for protesting. Within weeks, the Kennedy administration introduced what became the Civil Rights Act.

events.title: Medgar Evers Assassinated
events.blurb: The NAACP's field secretary in a Southern state was shot in the back in his own driveway as he returned home at 12:30 AM from a meeting, carrying T-shirts that read "Jim Crow Must Go." He died in front of his wife and three children. His killer, a Ku Klux Klan member, was tried twice; both trials ended in hung juries with all-white panels. He walked free for 31 years.
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1963 — Jackson, Mississippi. His killer, Byron De La Beckwith, was finally convicted in 1994 after new witnesses came forward. Medgar's widow Myrlie Evers-Williams spent decades pursuing the case; she later chaired the NAACP.

events.title: Malcolm X Assassinated
events.blurb: A charismatic Black Muslim minister who had broken with the Nation of Islam a year earlier was shot 21 times by three gunmen as he rose to address an audience at a Harlem ballroom. He was 39. The three men convicted of the killing included two who were demonstrably not at the scene; their convictions were overturned in 2021 after a decades-long campaign by their families and a Netflix documentary.
events.revealBlurb: February 21, 1965 — Audubon Ballroom, Manhattan. Malcolm had suffered an assassination attempt at his home a week earlier. His autobiography, co-written with Alex Haley and published posthumously, remains required reading in American universities.
